also: can I help you? — just looking

evidence: Plaut. Most. 753–754: ut sibi licēret īnspicere hasce aedīs tuās. — Nōn sunt vēnālēs.
terms.comment: A description of ours. Īnspicere is the buyer’s verb for looking a thing over before buying it (Lewis & Short: “to look at, inspect a thing with reference to its value”). In Plautus a man asks leave to look over a house and is told that it is not for sale. In Traupman it is the shopkeeper’s question, Quid vīs īnspicere?, and modo, “only”, makes the answer. We have found no set phrase for this in the authors we searched or in Traupman, Morgan–Owens, or Levi–Bini.

phrases.english: I’m not buying anything just now; I’m only looking.
What would you like to look at?

phrases.latin: quācumque libīdō est, incēdō sōlus, percontor quantī holus ac far
phrases.english: wherever I fancy, I stroll alone and ask what greens and flour cost

phrases.latin: ūndecimā lassus cum jam discēderet hōrā, asse duōs calicēs ēmit et ipse tulit.
phrases.english: When at the eleventh hour, worn out, he was finally leaving, he bought two cups for a penny and carried them home himself.
